strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in repository-aware code generation: improving completion quality while moving expensive context construction outside the interactive inference path. Combining cached retrieval with speculative implementations is a practical and clearly motivated contribution.

The reported improvements are substantial: on 980 REPOCOD tasks, SpecAgent reaches 27.86% and 27.96% pass@1, compared with best baseline scores of 17.65% and 18.88%. Evaluation uses executable tests, two completion models, and an additional agent backbone in Appendix A.

The retrieval-only, forecasting-only, and context-composition ablations provide useful evidence that the two components can complement each other. The paper also explicitly investigates temporal leakage and acknowledges limitations of synthetic repository states.
weaknesses: The central claim of a leakage-free benchmark is not established, and the construction example raises a concrete counterexample. Appendix C replaces color_palette with a newly introduced _process_palette helper that retains closely matching arguments and implementation branches, while rewriting callers to use it. This can transfer target-derived behavior into the supposedly earlier repository rather than remove it. Appendix B validates states only through an agent-assigned score of at least 4/5, without reporting independent audits, residual leakage rates, or executable validation results. The prevalence and performance impact of such replacements must be established before the main accuracy results support the claimed setting.

The comparisons confound retrieval method with repository state. Baselines use the original inference-time repository, whereas the proposed agents use synthetically edited repositories. Although the former may contain helpful callers, the latter can contain newly synthesized helper implementations, so the comparison is not demonstrably conservative. All methods should additionally be evaluated on the same validated repository states, with the source of the completion model's left/right context explicitly specified.

The temporal-leakage argument is too categorical. Tests and callers can legitimately precede implementations in test-driven or interface-first development. Their presence is not inherently leakage without a specified development timeline. Conversely, reconstructing an earlier state with an agent that sees the target does not establish historical plausibility. Evaluation on real pre-change snapshots, or a carefully audited subset, is needed to support the broader realism claims.

Reproducibility details are insufficient for the agent-dependent contribution. The manuscript does not provide the actual retrieval, forecasting, removal, and scoring prompts; precise agent model versions and sampling settings; tool-call budgets; ranking rules; or reproducible access to the generated repository states. Retrieval chunking and indexing configurations are also underspecified. Appendix D provides a completion prompt example, but this does not reproduce the critical preprocessing pipeline.

The latency evidence supports avoiding online retrieval, but not the broader claim of no additional inference-time cost. In Table 1, SpecAgent takes 4.55 versus 4.03 seconds without retrieval for Qwen3-8B, and 5.89 versus 5.03 seconds for Qwen3-30B-A3B; its advantage over BM25 for the latter is only 0.14 seconds. The approximately 50-second preprocessing cost lacks a clear accounting of both agents, repository-wide scaling, cache reuse, and invalidation under edits. Latency distributions, measurement details, and optimized retrieval configurations are needed to substantiate practical responsiveness.

Several reporting inconsistencies weaken confidence in the secondary evidence. Table 5 reports 39.99 seconds of latency for Qwen3-8B SpecAgent despite claiming comparable latency; its 20.20% accuracy also differs from the 21.63% three-prediction configuration in Table 8 without explanation. No repeated-run uncertainty or repository-level breakdown is supplied, and the 0.10-point advantage of three over one prediction block in Table 4 does not establish a reliable optimum.

Overall, the approach is promising, but benchmark validity and reproducibility concerns prevent a sound Findings recommendation. A next-cycle revision should prioritize auditing target-derived replacement code, controlled comparisons on shared repository states, and releasing the preprocessing artifacts and configurations.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in repository-aware code generation: moving expensive context construction outside the latency-critical completion path. Combining cached retrieval with speculative implementations is a practical, clearly motivated contribution.

The reported accuracy improvements are substantial. On 980 REPOCOD problems, SpecAgent improves pass@1 from the strongest baseline’s 17.65% to 27.86% for Qwen3-8B, and from 18.88% to 27.96% for Qwen3-30B-A3B. Execution-based evaluation provides meaningful evidence of completion quality.

Retriever-only, forecaster-only, context-composition, and inference-time ablations help investigate the design. Appendix A also evaluates another agent backbone, providing some evidence that the approach extends beyond Claude.
weaknesses: The central claim of a leakage-free benchmark is not established, and the paper’s own example raises a concrete counterexample. Appendix C removes color_palette but introduces _process_palette, preserving visible portions of the target’s implementation and adapting its callers. This can transfer target-derived information into the supposedly earlier repository state rather than eliminate it. Appendix B validates states only through an agent’s score of at least 4/5, without an independent leakage audit, measured residual leakage, or reported functional-test results. This undermines a central premise of the evaluation.

The comparison does not isolate method effects from repository-state effects. Baselines retrieve from the original inference-time repository, whereas the proposed agents use edited synthetic states. Although the authors intend this to disadvantage their agents, the edits can also introduce useful replacement implementations or remove distracting content; their effect is not necessarily conservative. All methods should additionally be evaluated on identical cleaned snapshots with matched context budgets. Table 3 partially addresses comparison under the original setting but does not validate the main cleaned-benchmark comparison.

The realism argument is overstated. Callers and tests can legitimately precede implementation in test-driven or interface-first development, so their presence does not universally constitute future leakage. Actual temporal provenance is needed to establish that distinction. Moreover, independently removing each target function does not demonstrate forecasting multiple future edits from a shared historical snapshot, cache reuse, or robustness as the repository evolves. The paper acknowledges synthetic-data limitations, but its strong deployment claims exceed the evidence.

The latency evidence supports eliminating online retrieval work, not uniformly reducing end-to-end latency. In Table 1, SpecAgent takes 5.89 seconds for Qwen3-30B-A3B versus 5.88 for BM25 + RepoMap and 5.03 without retrieval. The roughly 50-second preprocessing cost is insufficiently specified: Section 4 describes combining two agents, but the table reports a cost matching the slower individual agent without explaining concurrency or total compute. Repository-wide indexing costs, refresh frequency, amortization, latency distributions, and retrieval/prefill/generation breakdowns are missing.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the custom benchmark and agent pipeline. The manuscript provides examples but omits exact construction/scoring/retrieval/forecasting prompts, scoring rubrics, agent budgets and stopping rules, decoding settings, precise Qwen3-Coder identification, and several retrieval configuration details. It does not identify a release of the cleaned snapshots or implementation. Because repository editing and agent outputs are stochastic and central to the results, these omissions materially obstruct reproduction.

Several numerical inconsistencies require resolution. Table 5 reports 39.99 seconds for Qwen3-8B SpecAgent despite claiming comparable inference latency. Its three-prediction result is 20.20%, whereas Table 8 reports 21.63% for that composition without explaining the difference. No repeated-run uncertainty or paired significance analysis is provided; for example, Table 4’s 27.76% versus 27.86% does not convincingly establish three predictions as preferable to one.

The promising reported gains justify further consideration, but benchmark validity and reproducibility remain unresolved soundness concerns. These require substantive revision and controlled reevaluation before a Findings recommendation; the negative assessment is not based merely on limited novelty or subjective interest.

The retrieval-only, forecasting-only, and context-composition ablations provide useful evidence that retrieved evidence and predicted implementations can complement each other. Appendix A also evaluates a second agent backbone, although its gains are smaller.

Table 1 shows SpecAgent at 4.55 versus 5.01 seconds for BM25 with Qwen3-8B, but 5.89 versus 5.88 seconds for BM25 + RepoMap with Qwen3-30B-A3B; SpecAgent is slower than no retrieval for both models. Reproducibility is insufficiently specified for the agent-dependent benchmark and results. The manuscript lacks complete agent and scoring prompts, generation settings, exploration budgets, detailed retrieval configurations, and an artifact location for the transformed states and implementation. It reports no repeated-run uncertainty. Appendix A additionally contains unresolved numerical inconsistencies: SpecAgent’s Qwen3-8B latency is listed as 39.99 seconds despite the accompanying efficiency claim, and the three-prediction configuration scores 21.63% in Table 8 versus 20.20% in Table 5.

The paper treats callers and tests as necessarily unavailable before implementation, which excludes legitimate test-first and caller-first workflows. Its conclusions should be scoped to the chosen development scenario. Actual historical snapshots would provide stronger evidence of forecasting future additions than reconstructing individually deleted functions. Overall, the idea and reported gains are promising, but benchmark validity and reproducibility concerns prevent a sound Findings recommendation in the current version.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in repository-aware code generation: moving expensive context construction outside the latency-critical completion path. Combining cached retrieval with speculative implementations is a clear and practically motivated contribution.

The reported accuracy improvements are substantial: SpecAgent reaches 27.86% and 27.96% pass@1, versus the strongest listed baselines at 17.65% and 18.88%. Evaluation uses executable tests on 980 problems from 11 repositories.

Component and composition ablations provide evidence that retrieved evidence and predicted implementations are complementary. Additional experiments with Qwen3-Coder support some generality across agent backbones, although the gains are smaller.

The appendices provide extensive agent prompts, tool descriptions, context budgets, decoding settings, and examples. The paper also acknowledges limitations of synthetic repository histories and indexing costs.
weaknesses: The central leakage-free benchmark claim is not adequately established, and Appendix D presents a concrete counterexample to its rationale. Removing color_palette introduces _process_palette, whose displayed implementation reproduces portions of the removed function's logic, while callers retain corresponding usage patterns under the replacement name. This preserves precisely the semantic information the benchmark claims to eliminate. The scoring agent primarily checks remaining definitions and calls; its acceptance score does not establish absence of semantic leakage. Independent auditing, quantitative residual-leakage estimates, and evidence that remaining functionality is preserved are needed.

The evaluation tests reconstruction of a deliberately removed function rather than forecasting edits from a genuine earlier repository state. Agents are explicitly told that a function is missing, and each benchmark instance receives a separately modified snapshot. This can favor identifying artificial gaps and does not demonstrate that one cached context per file supports multiple subsequent developer edits. A historical or prospective evaluation, even on a smaller subset, would materially strengthen the central forecasting and amortization claims. Moreover, callers and tests can legitimately precede implementations, so their presence is not universally leakage.

Table 1 compares agents operating on cleaned snapshots with baselines operating on original, potentially leaky snapshots. Although the latter may give baselines additional information, this does not constitute a controlled comparison: repository transformations also change retrieval difficulty and available evidence. The same snapshots should be used for all methods. Appendix H additionally limits conventional retrieval to five 50-line chunks, whereas agents supply twelve flexible blocks; a common token ceiling alone does not establish comparable effective context budgets.

The latency conclusions exceed the measurements. SpecAgent is substantially faster than dense retrieval, but its 4.55/5.89-second latency exceeds the no-context baseline's 4.03/5.03 seconds and is not consistently better than RepoMap or BM25+RepoMap. Thus, eliminating online retrieval does not imply zero additional inference cost. The approximately 49-second preprocessing figure also requires clarification: SpecAgent combines two independently generated agent caches, yet reports the larger component time rather than their total compute. Parallel wall time, total token/cost consumption, repository-wide indexing, and actual reuse or refresh behavior should be distinguished.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting remain incomplete despite the detailed prompts. The manuscript provides no artifact access location for the stochastic, agent-modified snapshots or implementation, and does not fully specify agent model versions and sampling settings. Completion uses temperature 0.7 without reported repeated runs or confidence intervals. This particularly weakens fine-grained ablation conclusions, such as preferring three predictions over one by 0.10 percentage points. The Qwen3-Coder three-prediction result also differs between Table 7 (21.63%) and Table 8 (20.20%) without explanation.

These concerns affect the validity of the benchmark and the interpretation of the principal results, rather than merely novelty or prospective impact. The promising accuracy gains justify revision, but benchmark validation, controlled comparisons, and reproducible artifacts are needed before a sound Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in repository-level code completion: moving expensive context construction off the interactive inference path. Combining cached retrieval with speculative implementations is a coherent, potentially useful approach.

Table 1 reports substantial improvements across two completion models: 27.86% versus 17.65% pass@1 for Qwen3-8B, and 27.96% versus 18.88% for Qwen3-30B-A3B. Component ablations support the usefulness of combining retrieval and forecasting within the evaluated setup.

The appendices provide extensive agent prompts, implementation descriptions, decoding settings, and qualitative examples. Experiments with Qwen3-Coder provide additional evidence that the approach can benefit from another agent backbone.
weaknesses: The central leakage-free benchmark claim is contradicted by the construction example in Appendix D. After removing color_palette, the removal agent introduces _process_palette, preserving visible portions of the target's implementation, and rewrites callers to use this replacement. This transfers target-derived implementation and usage information into the supposedly earlier repository state. The example does not establish how widespread this problem is, but it directly undermines the benchmark's claimed guarantee and makes an independent audit and reevaluation necessary.

Benchmark validation is insufficient to resolve this concern. Appendices B.6 and C describe syntax checks and iterative LLM scoring focused on remaining definitions and calls. They report neither an independent semantic-leakage audit nor quantitative evidence that unrelated functionality remains correct. A score of at least four does not establish either property, especially when renamed replacement implementations can pass name-oriented checks.

The comparison does not isolate method effects from repository-state effects: baselines retrieve from the original inference-time repository, whereas indexing agents explore an agent-modified repository. Although the authors argue that this favors baselines, rewriting code can introduce useful synthesized evidence, so that direction is not guaranteed. All methods should also be compared on identical, independently validated snapshots. Moreover, callers and tests can legitimately precede implementations in test-first or caller-first development; their presence is not universally leakage.

The latency conclusions exceed the measurements. Table 1 shows SpecAgent taking 4.55 seconds versus 4.03 without retrieval for Qwen3-8B, and 5.89 versus 5.03 for Qwen3-30B-A3B; its advantage over BM25 for the larger model is only 0.14 seconds. Eliminating online retrieval does not eliminate context-processing overhead. Timing boundaries, uncertainty, and realistic serving conditions need clarification. The reported 49.08-second preprocessing time also needs to explain how both independently executed component agents are accounted for.

The deployment claim remains untested: contexts are generated for target-specific, function-removed snapshots, rather than reused across multiple actual future edits from one historical snapshot. There is no measurement of cache longevity, refresh frequency, repository-wide indexing cost, or amortization across completion requests. The current evidence primarily supports synthetic missing-function reconstruction.

Reproducibility and result consistency need improvement. The manuscript does not identify an accessible release of the modified snapshots or implementation, and omits agent sampling settings, exact Qwen3-Coder variant, and repeated-run uncertainty despite stochastic decoding. Table 7 reports 21.63% for three prediction blocks, whereas Tables 5, 6, and 8 report 20.20% for the apparent default configuration without explaining the difference. These concerns, particularly benchmark validity, prevent a sound Findings recommendation at present.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in repository-aware code generation: improving completion quality while moving expensive context construction outside the interactive inference path. The combination of cached retrieval and speculative implementations is clear and practically motivated.

Table 1 reports substantial improvements on 980 REPOCOD problems: SpecAgent reaches 27.86% and 27.96% pass@1, compared with the strongest listed baselines at 17.65% and 18.88%. Component and composition ablations provide evidence that combining retrieval with forecasting helps.

Experiments include two completion models and an additional indexing-agent backbone. The appendices provide extensive prompts, context examples, decoding settings, and implementation details that help readers understand the approach.
The paper recognizes an important temporal-evaluation issue and explicitly acknowledges that synthetic repository snapshots may differ from actual development histories.
weaknesses: The central claim of a leakage-free benchmark is not established, and Appendix D.2 provides a concrete counterexample. When removing color_palette, the cleaning agent introduces _process_palette, which retains target-related implementation logic, and rewrites callers to use it. This can transfer information about the removed functionality into newly generated, retrievable code rather than eliminate it. The scoring rubric in Appendix B.6 primarily checks definitions and calls, so it does not adequately detect this semantic leakage. An independent audit and evaluation after preventing such transfers are necessary; this is the decisive concern behind my recommendation to resubmit.

The experimental comparison mixes repository states: conventional baselines retrieve from the original inference-time repository, whereas SpecAgent retrieves from agent-edited snapshots. Although the former retain additional information, the latter may contain newly synthesized solution-relevant helpers, so the comparison cannot simply be characterized as conservative. Evaluating all methods on the same validated snapshots would make the accuracy gains more interpretable.

The deployment claims exceed the evidence. Each benchmark instance receives a target-specific removal snapshot, and the prompts explicitly ask agents to reconstruct a missing function. This differs from forecasting unspecified future edits in an evolving repository. There is no evaluation of cached context reuse across successive edits, context staleness, or refresh frequency. Moreover, callers and tests can legitimately precede implementations, so treating their presence as inherently unrealistic is too broad.

Latency improvements are conditional. In Table 1, Claude-based SpecAgent is slower than no-context and RepoMap completion for both models; for Qwen3-30B-A3B, its 5.89 seconds is essentially the same as BM25 + RepoMap at 5.88 seconds. Eliminating retrieval calls does not establish zero additional end-to-end cost. The roughly 49-second preprocessing figure also needs explicit accounting for both component agents, their parallel execution, total compute, and repository-wide indexing. Latency distributions and amortization measurements would strengthen the practical claims.

Some reporting and reproducibility gaps remain despite the detailed appendices. Table 7 reports 21.63% for three prediction blocks with Qwen3-Coder, while Table 8 reports 20.20% for the apparently corresponding configuration. Generation uses stochastic decoding, but repeated-run uncertainty is not reported. The manuscript also does not identify a release location for the edited snapshots and cached contexts, which are especially important because benchmark construction itself is stochastic.
